proposed.text: An architect must select a fire protection system for exposed structural steel beams in a 4-hour fire-resistive assembly (Type V construction). According to PD 1096 Rule VI, Sec. 603, which system achieves the 4-hour rating at the minimum thickness?

options.text: Concrete encasement at 75 mm — the densest material provides the best protection at minimum thickness, though it may add significant weight to the structure
Solid masonry encasement at 100 mm — masonry is the most durable and robust option, but requires additional structural support
Metal lath with vermiculite/perlite gypsum plaster at 50 mm — the most thermally efficient system achieves 4-hour rating at minimum thickness
All three systems achieve the 4-hour rating at the same thickness since they are all tested to the same performance standard, though practical application may vary

proposed.rationale: Original question was already source-correct and substantive; the prior edit (source-audited-article-batch-048) was degenerate, with 1-character garbage in 3 of 4 option text fields and a nonsensical rationale. Restored the original verbatim. Original source rationale: The material efficiency hierarchy for metal protection: plaster (thinnest) → concrete → masonry (thickest). Thermal efficiency is determined by microstructural void geometry, not bulk density. Vermiculite/perlite's microscopic pores create superior insulation at minimal thickness.
